title: Looking slowly
summary: A small invitation to notice one thing at a time.
body:
You do not have to learn the whole sky at once.

Begin with one name, one shape, or one question. Let the next small idea arrive tomorrow.

title: Why does Betelgeuse look red?
summary: A colour can become a clue to the life of a star.
body:
A familiar pattern can hold a new question. Find Orion's belt, then look towards the reddish point at one shoulder: Betelgeuse.

A star's colour gives us a clue to its surface temperature. Blue stars have hotter surfaces than red stars. A reddish star is still fiercely hot; cooler does not mean cold.

Betelgeuse is a red supergiant. The name describes a huge, expanded star with a relatively cool surface. Its size and colour tell different parts of its story.

A star also changes during its life. The rule about heavier stars burning hotter describes their long, steady stage. A red supergiant has moved beyond that stage. An enormous red star therefore does not undo what you learned about blue stars.

The hunter's outline helps us remember where to look. The stars themselves are real objects, with lives far beyond the picture. Lines drawn between them do not mean that they sit beside each other in space.

Next time you return to the chart, begin with the belt. Then find Betelgeuse. You now have a pattern to recognise and a question that colour can help answer.
